cells.tense: You are adjusting the give and take as it moves, and it is moving well today.
cells.ask: Offer one person a clear swap this week and let their answer change the shape of it.
cells.core:
You can feel when the give and take is off, and you're not doing arithmetic about it. Someone's short this week, someone's long, and you adjust without keeping score. People can tell, and they bring what they have to the table. Nothing is being counted and nothing is being owed.

The ease is real and it holds one edge: when it can't be repaired, you'll want to keep compensating past the point where the swap is already done. What keeps this workable is standing in today's exchange, not tomorrow's. If your read of the room is right, offer one trade plainly this week — no hedge in it — and take the answer you get as information, not a verdict on you.
cells.sheetLine: You adjust the balance as it moves, without keeping score.
cells.verb: calibrating the give and take until what's out of proportion comes back level
cells.place: the point of live adjustment between people, where the flow gets kept

cells.tense: You are keeping accounts for a day that hasn't arrived, bracing against what you'll be owed.
cells.ask: Pick one exchange you've been tracking and say the bare truth about it out loud, once.
cells.core:
You're running the numbers on things that haven't happened yet. Who'll owe you, who you owe, what the score will be by then — the ledger is being updated ahead of the conversation. The caring is still there. The room you're in with the other person isn't.

A running ledger makes every kindness look like a transaction, and it's exhausting to keep open. You don't have to close the account; just name one thing in it, plainly, without asking for anything back. Even if you're off about how bad the imbalance is, saying what you're counting gives the other person something to answer.

cells.tense: You are standing at a door already behind you, accepting arrangements that don't hold much for you today.
cells.ask: Next time a small thing comes up short, say one plain sentence of what you want before you agree.
cells.core:
You take the short end more often than the situation calls for. Not because you can't see it — you see it fine — but because asking for your share has felt like the thing that starts trouble. So you let the arrangement stand, and the person across from you doesn't learn what you wanted.

What's starved isn't your generosity; it's the ordinary practice of saying what you're owed when it's small. That practice can live somewhere quiet and low-stakes — one plain sentence when a small thing is short — and by the time the stakes are higher, the sentence will be there to reach for. None of this depends on getting the answer you want.
cells.sheetLine: You take the short end and leave what you wanted unsaid.

cells.tense: You are tallying grievances you didn't know you were counting, in a room you think you're just sitting in.
cells.ask: Say one of the tallies out loud this week — to the person, or even just alone in the car.
cells.core:
You're already weighing it. Somewhere you've been keeping a rough count of who gave what and who didn't, and you'd say you're not the type. The counting is doing its work in the background — shaping how you answer, what you offer, how far you lean in — and it hasn't been claimed as yours.

That's the whole gap: the tally is running and you're calling it just how things are. Name one entry, even half-formed, and it becomes something you can stand next to instead of something you stand inside. You may find the count is wrong, or smaller than it felt. Either way the pen is back in your hand.
